questions.stem: Because the aging publisher had never publicly {1} a successor, his empire fell to be fought over by a circle of {2} whose decades of deference had left none of them fit for independent command.
questions.explanation: Anoint is the verb for singling out a chosen successor and handing over the aura along with the office; deify would make the successor a god rather than an heir, and depose is the opposite motion, removal rather than selection. The second blank must name devoted servants whose loyalty outran their judgement — acolytes — since neophytes would be newcomers, which contradicts 'decades of deference,' and adversaries contradicts deference altogether.

questions.stem: Blackmail is objectionable twice over: it is {1} in its motive, since the blackmailer wants nothing beyond money, and it operates by {2}, since the victim's consent, real enough on paper, has been hollowed out in advance by threat.
questions.explanation: Base is the character verdict passed on a motive — greed, spite, cowardice measured against a code of honour — whereas abject describes wretchedness or self-abasement, not a mercenary motive, and inscrutable would deny that the motive is plain. The second clause describes a choice that is formally made but emptied out by threat, which is precisely coercion; suasion is the persuasion coercion replaces, and stealth would mean the victim never knew.

questions.stem: Constitutional lawyers keep the two cases apart: an assembly may lawfully {1} a new monarch when the throne falls vacant, but an abdication signed with troops in the antechamber is void for {2}, whatever the parchment records.
questions.explanation: Only anoint fits the lawful elevation of a new monarch to a vacant throne; relegate demotes and depose removes an incumbent, both the reverse of the act described. Troops in the antechamber make the signature a product of applied threat — coercion — rather than of carelessness (negligence) or unclear drafting (ambiguity).

questions.stem: For all the grandeur of its published aims, the expedition rested on motives no less {1} than the wish to strip a conquered province of its silver.
questions.explanation: Base and sordid both convict a motive of moral lowness — greed dressed up as grandeur — and yield sentences of the same meaning. Abject denotes wretchedness or grovelling rather than mercenary meanness; lofty reverses the sense, and obscure and pragmatic fit the grammar while asserting something quite different about the motives.

questions.stem: The court set aside the confession, holding that a statement extracted after eleven hours of questioning without counsel is the product of {1} rather than of conscience.
questions.explanation: Coercion and duress both name a decision compelled by pressure or threat, and either makes the confession legally worthless in the same way. Suasion is the persuasion the sentence rules out; exhaustion and deliberation are grammatically comfortable but describe a physical state and a considered choice respectively, neither of which is a ground for voiding the statement.

questions.stem: The seminar's atmosphere discouraged dissent: the professor was ringed by {1} who repeated his formulations back to him and treated any objection as a species of impiety.
questions.explanation: Acolytes and disciples both denote followers whose devotion has displaced independent judgement, which is exactly what the impiety clause describes. Neophytes would assert inexperience rather than devotion — the sentence says nothing about how long these people have been there — while skeptics and rivals contradict the deference, and functionaries points to administrative office instead of belief.

questions.stem: Though the party's rules still required a ballot, everyone understood that the retiring chancellor's endorsement would effectively {1} his successor, transferring an aura of legitimacy that no vote could confer.
questions.explanation: Anoint is the word for designating a chosen successor so that the choice reads as ordained rather than merely decided — the transfer of aura is its signature. Canonize declares a saint and venerate merely reveres someone already in place; neither selects an heir, and relegate and depose move in the opposite direction.

questions.stem: For thirty years he had been less a colleague than an {1}: he handled the director's correspondence, echoed his verdicts in committee, and was never once recorded as having disagreed with him.
questions.explanation: The details are all attendance and unquestioning service, which is what acolyte names — the follower whose function is to serve and whose loyalty has outrun independent judgement. A protégé is being groomed and would eventually stand on his own, a neophyte would be new rather than thirty years in place, and adversary and arbiter both imply an independence the sentence explicitly denies.
